Skandh Order Systems: Choosing a Way to Market

A teaching case on what a go-to-market strategy is. Skandh Order Systems and every person in it are fictional.

1. Opening

On the morning of Tuesday, 6 October 2026, Bhupendra Dhameliya sat in the second-floor office of Skandh Order Systems in Rajkot with two documents open. One was a spreadsheet of a 90-day pilot. The other was an email from a manufacturer in Morbi offering him, in effect, nine hundred customers at once. The email carried a deadline: an answer by Tuesday, 20 October, fourteen days away. Diwali fell on 8 November, nineteen days after that, and the weeks around it are when tile and sanitaryware dealers place their heaviest orders of the year.

Bhupendra, the founder, had a product that worked. He lacked settled answers to four questions: whom to sell to, through what route, in what order, and at what price. He had about ₹20 lakh of budget for the next twelve months, and he could not spend it in three directions at once.

2. Company background

Skandh Order Systems was founded in 2022 and sells a phone-and-desktop application called Falak Order Desk. It replaces the register, the WhatsApp voice note and the phone call by which most ceramic-tile and sanitaryware orders still travel in Gujarat. A dealer in Wankaner or Junagadh picks tiles by size and finish, the order is confirmed against the distributor's stock, and the invoice is raised in a GST-compliant format, including the e-way bill for the truck.

Morbi, roughly 65 kilometres from Rajkot, is the centre of Indian ceramic manufacturing, and its factories supply the wholesale and dealer network that also carries national names such as Kajaria, Somany and Johnson for tiles, and Cera, Hindware and Jaquar for sanitaryware. Most distributors keep books in Tally or Vyapar and talk in WhatsApp; the real competitor is habit. Skandh had eleven employees, a product built mostly in Pune, and monthly recurring revenue of a little under ₹2 lakh before the pilot began.

3. The situation

On 15 June 2026 the company opened a pilot across three kinds of customer, and on 13 September, the ninetieth day, the numbers were counted. Exhibit 1 sets them out. The pilot admitted 510 accounts and 135 were paying at day 90, a conversion of 26.5 per cent. The average hides a wide spread: 45 per cent of the 60 distributors paid, 32 per cent of the 150 mid-sized dealers, and only 20 per cent of the 300 small retail shops. The pilot brought in ₹7.50 lakh of monthly recurring revenue, of which the distributors alone account for ₹4.86 lakh, about 65 per cent.

Of the 48 paying dealers, nearly all had come through a distributor who was already using the product, about 1.8 dealers for each of the 27 paying distributors. The distributor is the gate, and retail shops mostly sit behind dealers.

The team saw the same facts from different places. Ishita Vadaliya, who leads product from Pune, worried that a rushed push into thousands of small shops would flood support with people who could not set up stock lists. Onil Ranpariya, the customer-success lead in Singapore, two and a half hours ahead of Rajkot, reviewed support tickets each evening and found retail shops the costliest to support per rupee of fee.

4. The people

Bhupendra Dhameliya, founder and chief executive, Rajkot. He wants growth that does not exhaust the company's ₹20 lakh and that leaves him free to negotiate with other manufacturers later.

Urvi Kotecha, sales head, Morbi. She wants distributors first. She has two representatives and estimates that they can bring on six distributors a month, because each needs about three weeks of on-site setup.

Ishita Vadaliya, product lead, Pune. She wants the product to be stable before volume arrives,.

Onil Ranpariya, customer success, Singapore. He wants to protect retention.

5. The offer from Morbi

The email came from Chinh Vitrified Ltd, a Morbi manufacturer whose 900 dealers place orders by phone. It proposed that Falak Order Desk become its mandatory ordering channel, at ₹600 per dealer per month, on the condition that Skandh serve no other manufacturer's dealer network in Gujarat for two years. Chinh's own estimate was that 40 per cent of dealers, or 360, would activate in the first year. The proposed fee is 85 per cent below the ₹4,000 that pilot dealers were paying.

Exhibit 3 places that offer beside two alternatives, sized to the pilot's economics. Spend for the first option uses the pilot's ₹20,000 per distributor; the third uses the pilot's ₹1,000 per retail shop and its 20 per cent conversion; the second uses Skandh's estimate of ₹1,250 per activated dealer for onboarding.

Exit monthly revenue is the month-twelve run rate, not revenue earned during the year. A: 72 distributors is six a month for twelve months. C needs about 2,500 shops entering the flow at 20 per cent conversion.

6. The options

Option A: distributors first. Urvi's team wins 72 distributors over the year. It has the largest exit revenue, ₹12.96 lakh a month, and it fills the referral engine that Exhibit 2 showed to be cheap. Its cost is ₹14.40 lakh, most of the budget, and it depends on people whose time is limited to six setups a month.

Option B: the Chinh mandate. It gives immediate reach and a manufacturer's name on the product. But it yields ₹2.16 lakh a month, less than a fifth of Option A's revenue, it anchors dealer pricing at ₹600, and the two-year exclusivity shuts out every other Morbi manufacturer.

Option C: self-serve to retail shops. It has the best return per rupee, 1.20 against 0.90 for Option A, and asks the least of Urvi's team. But it needs about 2,500 shops to enter the flow, the shops are the customers Onil finds hardest to support, and they mostly sit behind dealers who are not yet on the product.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Using Exhibit 1, which customer type gives the strongest evidence of demand, and what does the referral pattern say about who really decides?

2. In Exhibit 2, every route recovers its cost within about a month. Why is that not enough to choose Option C, the cheapest?

3. What is Chinh really buying at ₹600 and two years of exclusivity, and what does Skandh give up besides revenue?

4. Which target, route, timing and price would you set for the next twelve months, and what would make you change it?

8. A note for the learner

A go-to-market strategy is the plan for executing the acquisition section of the product strategy: who to target, how to reach them, when, and at what price. It is not a list of channels. Its test is whether the four answers agree with each other. Here they do not yet, and the three options each fix one answer while breaking another.

One defensible path. Choose Option A as the primary plan, and let it feed the cheaper routes rather than compete with them. Target distributors in the Rajkot, Morbi and Wankaner belt now, because they pay the highest fee, 45 per cent of them converted, and they bring dealers with them. Keep the ₹18,000 distributor price and the ₹4,000 dealer price, so that no early customer anchors the market lower. Hold roughly ₹5.60 lakh of the ₹20 lakh in reserve, which is what remains after Option A's ₹14.40 lakh, for the dealer referral programme and a small self-serve trial.

Decline the exclusive Chinh mandate by 20 October. Offer instead a non-exclusive arrangement in which Chinh's dealers may join at the standard dealer price through their existing distributors. This keeps other Morbi manufacturers reachable and the price intact. Revisit a mandate model once Skandh has 40 distributors live, when its bargaining position is stronger and Ishita's setup flow has been tested at scale. Option B fails on price and exclusivity, Option C on sequence, since shops mostly follow their dealers and their distributors. Option A is the only one whose four answers agree.

What a GTM Strategy Is

Who do we target, how, when, and at what price — and why the answer is a set of decisions that must be made together, not four separate memos.

1. The Tuesday before the board meeting

On the second Tuesday of March 2026, Meera Iyer, vice-president of product at Gavaksh Analytics, a Bengaluru-based maker of supply-chain visibility software, sat in a glass-walled meeting room with a slide she had rewritten four times. Gavaksh's flagship product tracked shipments and inventory for mid-sized manufacturers, and the company had spent the past nine months building a new module called TrackLens, which used sensor and GPS data to predict delivery delays before they happened. Engineering had finished it three weeks early. The board meeting was in six days, and the founders wanted to announce a launch date on the call.

The problem was not whether TrackLens worked — a pilot with two customers had cut late-delivery penalties by 31% in eleven weeks. The problem was that three people in the room wanted three different launches. The head of sales, Arvind Nair, wanted to sell TrackLens only to Gavaksh's twenty largest accounts, each doing more than ₹500 crore in annual revenue, at ₹1.2 lakh a month with a dedicated onboarding team, because that was where his team already had relationships. The head of growth marketing wanted a self-serve sign-up at ₹15,000 a month aimed at the thousand-odd small manufacturers who used Gavaksh's free shipment tracker but had never bought anything from a human being. And the co-founder, watching the runway, wanted whichever version reached ₹1 crore in monthly recurring revenue fastest, without much of a view on which one that would be.

Meera's job was not to pick a favourite. It was to notice that sales, marketing and the co-founder were each answering a fragment of a single question and calling their fragment the whole answer. Segment, price and channel are not three separate choices a company gets to make on three separate days; they are three faces of one decision, and getting two of them right while getting the third wrong can sink a product that everyone agrees is good. That single decision is what a go-to-market strategy is, and what Meera had six days to write down properly.

2. The idea, defined plainly

A go-to-market strategy, usually shortened to GTM, is the specific, written answer to four linked questions about a product: which customers will we sell to first, through which channel will we reach and sell to them, at what price and packaging, and in what sequence will we expand from there. It is not a marketing plan, though it informs one; it is not a pricing model, though it includes one; and it is not a launch checklist, though it produces one. It is the connective decision that determines whether the product strategy — the document that says what the product is and why it will win — ever converts into revenue, because a product strategy describes value and a GTM strategy describes how that value gets captured from a specific buyer through a specific path.

The term itself is younger than most people assume. Sales and marketing plans existed long before anyone called them "go-to-market," but the phrase entered common management usage through enterprise software and management-consulting practice in the 1990s, sharpened considerably by Geoffrey Moore's 1991 book Crossing the Chasm, which argued that the customer a company sells to first is not a smaller version of its eventual mass market but a categorically different kind of buyer — one who will tolerate a rough product because they need the specific outcome badly enough. Moore's insight, still the spine of GTM thinking today, was that choosing the wrong first customer breaks a product's momentum even when the product itself is fine, because everything downstream — the sales pitch, the price, the support model, the word of mouth — gets built around the wrong person's needs and expectations.

McKinsey and other consulting practices formalised the discipline through the 2000s as software companies multiplied and needed a repeatable way to decide, for each new product or market, who to sell to and how, rather than re-litigating the question from instinct every time. By the 2010s, product-led growth companies added a further twist: the "channel" question no longer meant only sales reps or retail shelves, it could mean a free product that sells itself through use, which changes the mechanics but not the underlying four questions.

"A GTM strategy is the decision, made once and made explicit, about who we sell to first, how we reach them, what we charge, and what we do next — because a great product with an unclear answer to those four questions still fails to grow."

That is the sentence Meera could say in the board meeting without sounding glib, because it names the trap precisely: Gavaksh already had a product strategy for TrackLens. What it lacked was an answer to who buys it first, at what price, and how it is sold — and until that answer existed and was written down, Arvind's plan, marketing's plan and the co-founder's revenue target would keep talking past each other.

3. The mechanics, walked through with TrackLens

A GTM strategy is built in a specific order, and skipping the order is the single most common way it goes wrong. The starting point is not the price and it is not the channel; it is the ideal customer profile, or ICP — a specific, falsifiable description of the customer for whom the product's value is largest and most urgent, not merely the customer who happens to be reachable. Meera's first move was to pull the pilot data: the two companies where TrackLens had cut late-delivery penalties by 31% were both mid-market auto-component manufacturers, revenue between ₹150 crore and ₹400 crore, shipping to three or more assembly plants, already paying penalty clauses that ran into the lakhs each quarter. That was a testable ICP, not a vague aspiration like "manufacturers who care about logistics."

The second step is choosing the channel — the mechanism by which the product reaches and is purchased by that ICP. Channel is not a marketing afterthought; it is constrained by how the ICP actually buys. A ₹500-crore manufacturer's plant-operations head does not discover new software through a Google ad and enter a credit card; the purchase runs through a procurement process with a demo, a security review, and a signature from someone two levels up. A small manufacturer's owner-operator, by contrast, might genuinely try a product for a week on a free trial before ever speaking to a salesperson. The ICP determines which channels are even available, which is why choosing segment before channel, rather than the reverse, is not a matter of taste.

The third step is price and packaging — not just a number, but the unit of value being sold (per shipment, per warehouse, per seat), the tiers, and what is included at each tier. Price is set with reference to the value the ICP receives (Gavaksh could point to real penalty-avoidance rupees) and to what the chosen channel can support economically: a channel that costs ₹1.5 lakh a month in sales-rep time cannot profitably sell a ₹15,000-a-month product, a mismatch that Arvind's plan, taken alone, never confronted.

The fourth step, the one practitioners most often skip because it feels like a later problem, is sequencing: which segment comes first, and what does success there unlock. Moore's chasm logic applies directly here — the first segment should be the one where the product's advantage is least deniable, even if it is not the largest market, because early wins there produce reference customers, sharpen the pitch, and pay for the next, harder segment. Meera's answer, once she laid the four steps out, was that Gavaksh's real choice was not "enterprise or self-serve" as a permanent either/or, but which one came first and funded the other.

Figure 1. A GTM strategy is not four independent choices; each decision narrows the next one. Gavaksh's finished answer for TrackLens is shown inside each box.

4. The arithmetic, worked twice

Meera's team pulled together the numbers behind three possible first segments for TrackLens, because a plan that sounds right in the room needs to survive contact with a spreadsheet. The exercise below is illustrative — built from Gavaksh's actual pilot and pipeline data, rounded for clarity — but the arithmetic is the kind any reader should be able to redo with their own numbers.

Table 1. Three candidate first segments for TrackLens, unit economics over a 30-month customer lifetime

The CAC figures are built from a simple model: a fully loaded inside-sales rep at Gavaksh cost roughly ₹1.5 lakh a month, and at steady state was closing two mid-market deals a month once ramped, giving a CAC of ₹75,000 per account. For SMB, a rep was not involved at all; the ₹25,000 CAC was blended content and performance-marketing spend divided by self-serve sign-ups. For enterprise, the field AE's time plus a 15% first-year commission paid to the systems-integrator partner who opened the door pushed CAC to ₹4.6 lakh per logo. On this first pass, mid-market wins clearly: an 18× LTV-to-CAC ratio comfortably clears the 3×-to-5× threshold that most software investors treat as healthy, and the 45-day cycle is short enough that Gavaksh's small sales team could carry a real pipeline without over-hiring.

The more useful exercise is the second pass, where Meera changed one input to see how fragile that conclusion was. Arvind had argued that if mid-market pricing were simply raised to ₹60,000 a month, TrackLens would generate more revenue per deal for the same sales effort. The arithmetic said otherwise. Raising price from ₹45,000 to ₹60,000 was estimated, from a small price-sensitivity test in the pilot group, to cut the close rate from roughly 16% of qualified leads to 11%, because plant-operations heads at that price point needed an extra sign-off that added friction and lost deals. At the same twelve qualified leads a month, that is 1.9 deals instead of 2, so the same ₹1.5-lakh rep now costs roughly ₹1.15 lakh in CAC per deal.

The higher price still produces more revenue and a healthy 12.5× ratio, so it is not a disaster — but it is worse on every efficiency measure, not better, because the CAC rose faster than the price did once conversion is accounted for. This is the habit a GTM strategy is meant to install: no single number, including price, can be judged in isolation from what it does to the conversion rate through the chosen channel. Meera's recommendation, in the end, kept the ₹45,000 price for the initial mid-market launch and treated ₹60,000 as a question for a later tier with more included, not a straight repricing.

5. The nuances a learner must sit with

GTM is not marketing, and treating it as marketing's job alone starves it of sales and product input

Because "go-to-market" contains the word "market," it is routinely handed entirely to the marketing function, which then owns messaging and channel spend but has no authority over price or the product roadmap. At Gavaksh, this had already happened once with an earlier product: marketing had built a beautiful self-serve funnel for a segment that, it turned out, needed a human in the sales process to get past a procurement gate marketing had no visibility into. A GTM strategy is cross-functional by construction — product, sales, marketing, and often legal or finance for anything involving contracts or regulated data — and a plan authored by one function alone is a symptom, not a strategy.

Segment is not the same as persona, and conflating them hides who actually signs

An ICP describes a company; a persona describes a person inside that company. TrackLens's ICP was mid-market auto-component manufacturers, but within that company at least three personas mattered differently: the plant-operations head who felt the pain daily, the CFO who owned the penalty line item and controlled budget, and the IT security lead who could block the deal on data-residency grounds regardless of what the other two wanted. A GTM plan that specifies the ICP but not which persona is the champion, the economic buyer and the blocker will produce a sales pitch aimed at whichever person happens to answer the phone, which is not a strategy.

A GTM strategy is not permanent, and mistaking the first answer for the final one causes a company to defend a beachhead past its usefulness

Moore's chasm logic is explicitly sequential: the first segment is chosen to be won, not to be the company's identity forever. Gavaksh's mid-market beachhead existed to generate references and revenue that would fund a harder, longer enterprise sales motion later, and eventually a lighter SMB motion once the product matured. Companies that never revisit segment, channel or price after the first success end up serving a market that has stopped growing while a larger one goes uncontested, simply because nobody scheduled the re-decision.

It cannot tell you whether the product itself is good

A GTM strategy answers who to sell to and how, not whether what is being sold deserves to exist. If TrackLens's predictions had not actually reduced penalties, no combination of segment, channel and price would have rescued it for long — a strong GTM strategy can accelerate a mediocre product's failure by getting it in front of unhappy customers faster and louder. The discipline assumes a product with real, demonstrated value as an input; it is a capture mechanism, not a value-creation one.

Channel and price are jointly constrained, and choosing them independently is the most expensive mistake on this list

It is tempting to pick the channel that feels prestigious (a direct enterprise sales team) and the price that feels ambitious (a premium number) without checking whether the two are compatible. A ₹15,000-a-month product cannot support a field sales team; a ₹1.2-lakh-a-month enterprise deal cannot be sold through a self-serve sign-up page, because the buyer needs a security review, a reference call and a signature that a webpage cannot provide. Every viable GTM plan is a matched pair of channel-cost and price, not two separately optimised choices.

"Who to target first" is not "who has the biggest budget"

Arvind's instinct to start with Gavaksh's twenty largest accounts was not unreasonable on its face — enterprise deals are larger. But the largest accounts also carry the longest sales cycles, the most demanding procurement processes, and the least tolerance for a first-version product with rough edges, exactly the profile Moore warned against leading with. The right first segment is the one where the product's advantage is starkest and the buying process is short enough to generate fast, repeatable proof, which is a different question from which segment could eventually generate the most revenue.

A GTM strategy answers "at what price," not "at what price forever"

The price set at launch is a hypothesis tied to a specific segment and channel, tested against real conversion data, as Table 2 showed. Confusing an initial price with a permanent one either freezes a company at an early number that undervalues a maturing product, or invites constant repricing driven by whichever executive spoke last in a meeting, rather than by a fresh version of the same segment-channel-price arithmetic.

The question a thoughtful newcomer should ask before relying on this idea: what is the evidence for the ICP, and is it a customer story or a spreadsheet?

Any team can produce a plausible-sounding ICP from intuition. The test of whether a GTM strategy is grounded is whether the ICP claim survives being checked against real usage, real pilot results or real win-loss data, the way Meera's ICP survived being checked against the two pilot customers' actual penalty-avoidance numbers. A GTM strategy built on an untested ICP is a guess wearing the vocabulary of a decision.

6. How this differs by product type and by company stage

In a consumer product, the "who" is usually a behavioural or demographic segment rather than a named company, the channel is overwhelmingly owned and paid digital media plus app-store discovery, and price is frequently zero at first contact, monetised later through subscription or advertising; the GTM question becomes less "who signs the contract" and more "which acquisition channel produces users who convert to paying without ballooning the marketing spend." In a B2B product like TrackLens, the who is a company with an internal buying committee, the channel runs through sales or partners because the purchase requires trust and configuration, and price is negotiated and tiered around real contract value, as the tables above show. In a marketplace product, the GTM question effectively doubles, because a marketplace must win two distinct sides — Gavaksh's later marketplace experiment connecting shippers with freight carriers, for instance, needed a separate ICP, channel and even price logic for carriers than for shippers, with sequencing questions (which side to seed first, and how to subsidise it) that a single-sided product never faces at all.

Figure 2. Channel is not a free choice: it follows from where a product sits on deal size and buying complexity. Gulzar Mart, a small consumer inventory app, sells itself through app-store discovery; Girnar Systems, an enterprise rival, needs a systems-integrator partner just to get in the door.

Stage matters as much as product type. An early-stage company like Gavaksh five years earlier had one product, one founder-led sales motion, and effectively one GTM decision to get right at a time; a larger, multi-product Gavaksh now had to coordinate TrackLens's GTM plan with the existing shipment-tracking product's sales team, who already had relationships with the same accounts and did not want a second, differently priced product complicating their pitch. Later-stage GTM strategy is as much about internal sequencing — which team sells what, and how a new product avoids cannibalising or confusing an existing one — as it is about the external customer.

7. Common mistakes

Mistake one: pricing before segmenting. The symptom is a price that was set in a competitive-benchmarking exercise before anyone could say precisely whose budget it was meant to come out of. The underlying misunderstanding is treating price as a market-wide number rather than a number tied to one ICP's willingness to pay for one specific outcome. The cheapest diagnostic: ask the person who set the price to name the exact job title of the buyer and the exact line item the price displaces in that buyer's budget; if they cannot, the price was set before the segment was.

Mistake two: choosing the channel the team is comfortable with, not the one the buyer needs. The symptom is a sales team pursuing self-serve sign-ups by cold-calling them, or a product team building a self-serve funnel for a buyer who has never once completed an online purchase over ₹50,000 without a phone call. The underlying misunderstanding is optimising for organisational convenience instead of the buyer's actual purchasing behaviour. The cheapest diagnostic: pull the last ten closed-won and closed-lost deals and trace, deal by deal, how the buyer actually engaged, not how the team intended them to.

Mistake three: launching to everyone at once because saying no to a segment feels like leaving revenue on the table. The symptom is a launch announcement with no named first customer type, aimed at "manufacturers" or "businesses" broadly. The underlying misunderstanding is that sequencing is a constraint imposed by limited resources rather than a deliberate choice that concentrates a small team's proof-generation where it is cheapest to win. The cheapest diagnostic: ask what the second segment is and what has to be true in the first one before the team moves to it; if there is no second segment planned, there was no sequencing, only spray.

Mistake four: treating the GTM plan as a one-time document rather than a set of numbers to be re-run. The symptom is a pricing page or a target-account list that has not changed in eighteen months despite the product changing considerably. The underlying misunderstanding is confusing the discipline (repeatable arithmetic) with the artefact (a slide from the launch). The cheapest diagnostic: ask when the CAC and LTV numbers behind the current plan were last recalculated with actual, not projected, data.

8. What good looks like

Two years after TrackLens launched, a different Gavaksh product manager, Rohan Desai, faced a similar decision for a new customs-clearance-prediction feature and handled it the way Meera's TrackLens work had set as the internal template. He did not start with a launch date; he started by pulling win-loss data from the previous eight months to identify which existing customers had asked, unprompted, for exactly this capability, arriving at an ICP of import-heavy mid-market manufacturers with at least two overseas suppliers. He priced the feature as an add-on to the existing mid-market TrackLens contract rather than as a new standalone product, at ₹12,000 a month, explicitly because it let the existing 45-day sales motion sell it without a new negotiation cycle, keeping CAC near zero for the installed base. He set a first-quarter target of twelve customers, not because twelve was impressive, but because it was exactly the number needed to produce three strong reference stories before opening the feature to a second, colder segment. When the actual conversion rate came in eight points below forecast in month two, he treated it as data to re-run the arithmetic, not as a reason to panic-discount the price. That is what a disciplined GTM strategy looks like in practice: an ICP grounded in evidence, a channel chosen for the buyer's behaviour rather than the team's comfort, a price matched to that channel's economics, and a sequence with a named next step.

9. What Meera decided, and what to learn next

Meera walked into the board meeting with a plan that disappointed both Arvind and the growth-marketing lead, and satisfied the co-founder more than either of theirs would have. TrackLens would launch first to the mid-market segment, sold through inside sales at ₹45,000 a month per plant, targeting eight to ten reference customers within the first two quarters before either the enterprise or the SMB motion was funded and staffed. Arvind's twenty largest accounts and marketing's self-serve funnel were not wrong ideas; they were the second and third segments, sequenced deliberately rather than launched simultaneously and starved of focus. The board approved it without much debate, mostly because the unit-economics table made the reasoning visible rather than asking anyone to trust an instinct.

The natural next things to learn, once this idea is solid, are the specific channel mechanics that a GTM strategy chooses between — paid, owned and earned acquisition for the marketing-heavy end, and the contrasting playbooks of product-led growth versus sales-led growth for the buyer-behaviour end of the spectrum — because "channel" in this page was treated as one decision, and it is really a family of distinct disciplines with their own mechanics and their own failure modes. Understanding those is what turns "we chose inside sales" into knowing exactly how to run inside sales well.

Two questions worth sitting with:

1. For a product you know well, can you name the ICP precisely enough that someone else could go find ten companies matching it without asking you a follow-up question — and if not, was the segment ever really chosen, or only described in retrospect?

2. If you raised your own product's price by 30% tomorrow, do you know which of your acquisition channels would break first, and would you find out from a spreadsheet or from a quarter of disappointing numbers?

What a GTM Strategy Is

Who to target, how, when and at what price — treated not as four questions but as a single feasibility problem, in which the binding constraint is almost never the one written on the slide.

1. Two rooms, ten days apart

On the morning of 14 April 2026, in a converted textile-mill office in Pune, Sudha Ramanathan sat with a printout of her own board pack and a pencil, striking through a line she had written herself. Sudha was chief product officer of Matsya Cold Chain Systems, a seven-year-old company that made a battery-powered temperature and humidity logger — the MCT-2, about the size of a paperback — together with the cloud service that turned the loggers' readings into excursion alerts, audit trails and the compliance reports that pharmaceutical distributors file when a consignment strays outside its permitted range. Matsya had 61 paying accounts, almost all of them pharmaceutical distributors and third-party cold-chain operators, an average of 220 devices per account, and a board that had just approved a plan to double the sales force.

The line Sudha was striking through read: “Expand direct field coverage from four to nine territories to capture the frozen-foods and quick-commerce dark-store segment.” She had written it in February and believed it in February. What had changed was not her view of the market, which remained large and real, nor her view of the product, which worked. What had changed was a single number that Ritu Bhandare, Matsya's finance head, had put in front of her the previous Thursday: the cumulative cash position of the average new account, month by month, from signature onward. Because Matsya gave the loggers away free and recovered their cost inside a ₹300-per-device monthly subscription, each new account began life as a ₹7.92 lakh cash outflow for hardware before a single rupee of the ₹4.4 lakh cost of winning it had been counted. The average account did not turn cash-positive until month 23 of a 36-month contract. Matsya was not selling software with a sales problem. It was running a lending business it had not noticed it was running, and the plan to double the sales force was, in cash terms, a plan to double the size of the loan book.

Ten days later and 150 kilometres away, in a co-working floor in Lower Parel, Kabir Sethi was arguing about something that looked entirely different and was structurally the same. Kabir had co-founded Munim AI eighteen months earlier; the product was an agentic bookkeeping assistant that connected to a business's accounting ledger and its GSTN filings, reconciled purchase invoices against input-tax-credit records, and flagged mismatches with a written explanation a human could check. It was genuinely good: in a sample of 400 workspaces, it had cut the median time to close a month's books from nine working days to two and a half. It had 11,400 self-serve sign-ups in the previous quarter, a free tier, and a conversion rate to the ₹4,000-a-month paid plan that Kabir's growth lead, Shalini Koppar, described as “respectable and completely beside the point.”

The point Shalini was making was that Munim's free tier was not free. Every active free workspace consumed roughly ₹180 a month in model inference, because reconciliation is a document-heavy task and the reasoning passes are long. Three thousand one hundred active free workspaces cost Munim ₹5.58 lakh a month in variable cost that appeared, correctly, in cost of goods sold rather than in the marketing line. The board looked at a 54% gross margin and asked why a software company had the margins of a distributor. The growth team looked at a five-month payback and said the funnel was healthy. Both were reading the same business and neither was wrong. What neither had yet said out loud was that Munim's cheapest, fastest and most reliable route to revenue ran through something Kabir actively did not want: the roughly 900 chartered-accountancy practices that already did the books for the very businesses Munim was trying to reach one at a time, each practice controlling 60 to 200 client relationships and each one perfectly capable of deciding, in a single conversation, that its clients would use somebody else's product instead.

Neither Sudha nor Kabir had a product problem, a pricing problem, a channel problem or a segmentation problem. Each had one problem wearing four costumes. The purpose of this page is to make that single problem precise, to show the arithmetic that exposes it, and to be honest about the parts of it the field has not settled.

2. The idea: a feasibility problem wearing the costume of four questions

A go-to-market strategy is conventionally defined as the answer to four questions: who do we sell to, through what channel, at what price and packaging, and in what sequence do we expand. That definition is correct and, at this level of study, insufficient, because it invites the reader to believe that the four are separately choosable. They are not. A more exact definition, and the one this page will defend, is this: a go-to-market strategy is the selection of a mutually feasible combination of segment, channel, price and sequence, under a set of constraints the firm does not control, together with the explicit identification of which constraint is binding. The four questions are not four decisions. They are four coordinates of one point, and most of the points in that four-dimensional space are infeasible — they describe combinations that cannot pay for themselves, cannot be executed by the organisation that exists, or cannot be bought in the manner they are being sold.

The word “feasible” is doing real work. A ten-crore enterprise deal sold through a self-serve sign-up page is infeasible not because it is unfashionable but because the buyer cannot complete a security review, a data-residency attestation and a two-signature purchase order on a web form. A ₹15,000-a-month product sold by a field representative earning ₹2.2 lakh a month is infeasible in the same hard sense: the arithmetic does not close, no matter how motivated the representative. Expertise in this topic consists almost entirely of the ability to identify, quickly and before spending money, which of the candidate combinations lie inside the feasible set — and then, among those, which one the firm can execute given who it has hired and what its cash position will tolerate.

What the idea was invented to fix

The intellectual lineage is older and less software-centric than the modern vocabulary suggests. Alfred Chandler's business-historical work, particularly Scale and Scope (1990), argued that the firms that dominated the second industrial revolution did so through a three-pronged investment — in production, in distribution, and in professional management — and that the second of these was routinely the decisive one. Chandler's claim, uncomfortable for product people, was that superior products lost to inferior products with better distribution often enough that distribution should be treated as a primary strategic asset rather than a downstream function. E. Jerome McCarthy's four Ps (1960) gave the decision a vocabulary; Theodore Levitt's “Marketing Myopia” (1960) supplied the warning that firms define their market too narrowly around what they make; Everett Rogers's Diffusion of Innovations (1962) supplied the observation that adoption proceeds through categorically different populations rather than uniformly.

Geoffrey Moore's Crossing the Chasm (1991) turned Rogers into an operating instruction: pick a beachhead segment narrow enough that word of mouth circulates within it, win it completely, and use it as the base for the next. Steve Blank's The Four Steps to the Epiphany (2005) added the taxonomy that is still the most under-used idea in the field — that a company is entering either an existing market, a resegmented market, a new market or a clone market, and that the correct go-to-market plan differs so radically across those four that borrowing a playbook across them is the most common unforced error in early-stage companies. Mark Leslie and Charles Holloway's “The Sales Learning Curve” (Harvard Business Review, 2006) supplied the first genuinely quantitative treatment of when a company may add sales capacity, an argument we will work through with numbers in the next section. Bill Aulet's Disciplined Entrepreneurship (2013) made beachhead selection an explicit sizing exercise. The phrase “product-led growth,” popularised from around 2016, named a channel that had existed for a decade without a label: the product itself, doing the work of demand generation.

Running against all of this is an empirical tradition that most product managers never encounter and that any expert should be able to state fairly. Byron Sharp and the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute, in How Brands Grow (2010), assembled decades of purchase-panel data to argue that brands grow overwhelmingly through penetration among light buyers, that loyalty differences between competing brands are small and largely a function of market share, and that narrow targeting is therefore usually a way of buying less growth for the same money. Les Binet and Peter Field's work on advertising effectiveness pointed in a similar direction with a different instrument: broad, emotionally-led brand building compounds over years, while narrowly-targeted activation produces sharp but non-cumulating spikes. Applied to business software, the LinkedIn B2B Institute's argument that only about 5% of a category's buyers are in market in any quarter implies that a go-to-market strategy tuned entirely to in-market buyers is optimising a small fraction of the available demand.

These traditions do not merely emphasise different things. They make incompatible claims about the same decision, and an expert should be able to say which claim they are relying on and what would have to be true for it to be wrong. The second is that in any real meeting, the participants will not name their school. Sudha's head of sales, Joseph Pinto, was a distribution-first thinker who had never read Chandler; Shalini Koppar at Munim was making a penetration argument in the language of funnel metrics. A practitioner who can hear the school underneath the argument can referee the meeting. One who cannot will experience it as a clash of personalities.

3. The mechanics, worked: the frontier, the learning curve and the cash shape

Competent practitioners choose a segment, then a channel, then a price. Expert practitioners run the same three decisions in a different order: they first establish which channels are financially feasible at all for a product of this margin and this contract size, because that single calculation eliminates most of the candidate strategies before anyone has to have an opinion. The calculation is not complicated, and it is worth doing arithmetically rather than describing.

Let C be the fully loaded cost of acquiring one customer through a given channel — not the marketing spend alone, but every rupee the channel consumes divided by the deals it closes: salaries, quota-carrier ramp time, sales engineering, travel, the marketing programmes that feed it, and any revenue share paid to a partner. Let m be the gross margin on the revenue that customer produces, net of any margin surrendered to a partner. Let p be the payback tolerance the firm can actually finance, expressed in years of gross profit. A channel is feasible for a product only if its annual contract value satisfies

ACV  ≥  C ÷ (m × p)

which rearranges to the observation that for a fixed payback tolerance, each channel traces a curve in the space of contract value and gross margin, with everything above the curve feasible and everything below it not. Three second-order effects hide inside that table and are the reason it is not merely a lookup. The first is that the margin surrendered to a partner is subtracted from m, not from ACV, and because m sits in the denominator its effect is non-linear: at 80% gross margin, giving a dealer 25% raises the feasibility threshold by 45%; at 45% gross margin, the same 25% share raises it by 180%. Partner economics that are merely expensive for a high-margin software product are lethal for a hardware-inclusive one. This is why the same reseller agreement can be a sensible growth lever at one company and an act of self-harm at another, and why “what margin do channel partners get in this industry?” is a question with no useful general answer.

The second effect is that the payback tolerance p is not a preference. It is set by the firm's access to capital and by the volatility of its retention. A firm that can borrow cheaply against contracted revenue, or that has just raised equity, can rationally run a two-year payback and will see feasible channels that a bootstrapped competitor cannot see. This is the most underappreciated reason why two companies selling near-identical products correctly adopt different go-to-market strategies: they face different p. It is also why the go-to-market argument in a company is so often unresolvable inside the product organisation. The binding constraint lives on the balance sheet.

The third effect is that C is not a constant but a declining function of the company's cumulative experience — and this is where the one genuinely quantitative model in the field earns its place.

The sales learning curve, applied to Matsya

Leslie and Holloway's argument is that a sales force in a new market is doing two jobs, and that companies routinely pay for the second while measuring the first. Early representatives are not primarily producing revenue; they are producing information — about which objection kills deals, which proof point moves a buying committee, which implicit qualification criterion separates the accounts that close from the ones that consume six months and vanish. Yield per representative therefore rises with the company's cumulative closed deals, slowly at first and then sharply, and the mistake is to add capacity during the flat part of the curve on the assumption that yield is a property of the representative rather than of the company's accumulated learning.

Matsya's own data made the shape visible. Its first eight accounts had taken an average of 3.5 representative-months each to close. Between the ninth and the twenty-fourth, that fell to 2.6. Across the most recent twenty accounts it was 2.0 — a steady-state yield of six accounts per representative per year. The break-even yield is straightforward to derive. A fully loaded field representative cost Matsya ₹2.2 lakh a month, or ₹26.4 lakh a year. Each account produced ₹7.92 lakh of annual revenue at a 45% gross margin, or ₹3.56 lakh of annual gross profit. Under a twelve-month payback rule, a representative must therefore close 26.4 ÷ 3.56 = 7.4 accounts a year to cover her own cost within the first year of the accounts she sells. Matsya's representatives were closing six.

That single comparison — 6.0 against 7.4 — is the whole board argument reduced to two numbers, and the reduction is instructive because of what it reveals about where the disagreement really sits. Under a twenty-four-month payback rule the required yield falls to 3.7 accounts a year, and the direct motion is not merely feasible but comfortable. Nothing about the customer, the product or the sales team differs between the two calculations. Only p differs. Joseph Pinto was not wrong that direct selling worked; Ritu Bhandare was not wrong that it could not be financed. They were arguing about the discount rate while believing they were arguing about strategy, which is among the most common patterns in real go-to-market disputes and among the easiest to defuse once named.

There is one further distortion that neither the frontier nor the learning curve captures, and it is the one that had made Sudha strike out her own recommendation. Ratios such as LTV to CAC and payback months are computed on accounting gross profit, which treats the hardware Matsya gave away as an expense amortised over the contract. Cash does not amortise. Matsya paid ₹3,600 per landed device, 220 devices per account, on the day of deployment: ₹7.92 lakh out the door before the first subscription invoice. Full attach would have raised the direct ACV to ₹10.3 lakh, which lifts the account above the field-sales curve in Figure 1. The direct motion is infeasible at today's attach rate and feasible at a plausible one. Whether to plan on the plausible one is a judgement about execution risk, not a calculation, and it is exactly the kind of judgement this topic exists to structure rather than to settle.

The same mechanics under AI-native cost structure

Munim's arithmetic differs in one structural respect that is worth isolating, because it is new enough that the conventional heuristics have not caught up with it. In classical software, the marginal cost of a free user is approximately zero, which is why the free tier was correctly treated as a marketing expense with an unusually favourable cost curve: doubling the top of the funnel doubled the sign-ups and barely moved cost of goods sold. In an inference-heavy product, the marginal cost of an active free user is not zero and not small. Munim's 3,534 activated free workspaces in the March quarter consumed ₹180 each a month; over the sixty-day window in which conversion occurs, that is ₹12.72 lakh of variable cost incurred to produce 219 paying customers.

The correct accounting treatment and the correct managerial treatment diverge here, and experts hold this divergence in mind deliberately. For the statutory accounts, inference on free workspaces is cost of goods sold and depresses reported gross margin. For the go-to-market decision, it is customer acquisition cost and belongs in CAC. Munim's blended CAC on the self-serve motion is therefore not the ₹9.4 lakh of quarterly marketing spend divided by 219, or ₹4,300, but (₹12.72 lakh + ₹9.4 lakh) ÷ 219 = ₹10,100. 4. When the idea applies, and when it actively misleads

Treating go-to-market as a designed feasibility problem is not universally appropriate, and the conditions under which it is appropriate can be stated as claims that are checkable in an afternoon. Six of them carry most of the weight.

First: the value of the product can be demonstrated to a stranger inside the length of the buying cycle. If it cannot — if the benefit only becomes visible after two years of accumulated data, or after an organisational change the buyer has not yet made — then no combination of segment, channel and price is feasible, and the correct work is product work, not go-to-market work. Matsya clears this test comfortably; a single excursion caught in the first month pays for a quarter of subscription. Munim clears it emphatically: a reconciliation run against a business's own last-month data produces a visible, checkable list of mismatches within twenty minutes, which is why its activation metric is a meaningful predictor of anything at all.

Second: the buying unit can be enumerated. An ideal customer profile is only operational if someone can produce a list of the firms or people who match it without asking the author a follow-up question. Matsya passes: the population of Indian pharmaceutical distributors and cold-chain third-party logistics operators with more than eight reefer vehicles is finite, knowable and roughly 1,900 firms. Munim passes on the channel side — the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India membership directory makes the practice population enumerable — but fails on its direct side, where “Indian SMEs that file GST returns” is a population of over fourteen million and therefore not a segment at all, merely a universe. This asymmetry is not incidental to Kabir's decision; it is most of it.

Third: the cost per deal through the candidate channel is measurable within one planning cycle. Channels whose cost can only be evaluated over three years — brand advertising, category creation, most conference sponsorship — cannot be arbitrated by the frontier calculation and must be justified on a different basis. Practitioners who insist on putting every channel through a payback test end up systematically underinvesting in the slow ones, which is one of the strongest points the penetration school makes against the performance-marketing orthodoxy.

Fourth: retention is long enough that acquisition economics dominate. Where the customer relationship is a single transaction or a highly promiscuous repeat purchase, the arithmetic above collapses, because LTV is not a stable quantity and the relevant competition is for the next purchase occasion rather than for the relationship. Matsya's three-year contracts and Munim's annual ones both satisfy the condition. A quick-commerce grocery application would not.

Fifth: the firm controls its own price. In categories where price is set by a regulator, a formulary, a marketplace ranking algorithm or a large customer's reverse auction, price is an input rather than a decision, and the go-to-market problem shrinks to segment, channel and sequence. Matsya encountered this in a muted form: when it sold into government-run vaccine cold chains, price came from a tender, and the whole apparatus of value-based pricing became irrelevant overnight.

Sixth: demand is not wholly determined by a gatekeeper the firm cannot influence. Where an app store, a platform's default setting, a hospital procurement consortium or a single dominant distributor controls access, go-to-market strategy becomes a negotiation strategy with that gatekeeper, and the language of segments and funnels obscures rather than illuminates what is happening.

Where the idea is not merely inapplicable but actively misleading is worth stating separately, because these are the situations in which a well-run go-to-market process produces confident, precise, wrong answers. The first is Blank's new-market case: when a company is creating a category, there is no baseline conversion rate, no established willingness to pay and no enumerable in-market population, so every input to the frontier calculation is a guess dressed as a measurement, and the apparatus lends the guess an authority it has not earned. The honest move in a new market is to run the process as a set of explicit bets with named falsifying observations, not as a model. The second is the high-frequency, low-consideration consumer case, where the penetration school's evidence is strongest and a tightly-drawn ideal customer profile can genuinely cost a brand growth by concentrating spend on buyers who would have bought regardless. The third is the supply-constrained case: when a firm cannot serve more demand than it already has, effort spent optimising acquisition is effort misallocated, and the correct response is to raise price until demand matches capacity — a move that go-to-market frameworks rarely surface because they are built to answer “how do we get more customers” rather than “should we.” The fourth is the capital-determined land grab, in which the winner is whoever can subsidise longest, and channel efficiency is a second-order variable that feels like a first-order one.

5. Hard edges: where the four-question framing breaks

The clean version of the problem assumes one product, one side of a market, one unconstrained pricing decision and one organisation that does what its plan says. Every one of those assumptions fails somewhere, and the failures are where expertise is actually tested.

Multi-product companies, where the scarce resource is internal

A single-product company competes for the customer's attention. A multi-product company competes for its own sales force's attention first, and the customer's second. When Manjeera Rail Systems, a Hyderabad firm selling signalling-maintenance software to metro operators and private freight rakes, launched a second product for wagon-utilisation analytics, its go-to-market plan named the same twenty-two accounts its first product already served. The plan was sound and the launch failed, because the account executives carried a single annual quota, the new product's average deal was one-fifth the size of the old one's, and every hour spent introducing it was an hour not spent on a renewal worth five times as much. No amount of enablement fixed this; changing the compensation plan to carve out a separate product quota fixed it in one quarter. The generalisable point is that in a multi-product firm, the compensation plan is a component of the go-to-market strategy with equal standing to price, and a plan that does not specify it has not been written. Mature companies know this and still get it wrong, usually because the compensation plan is owned by a sales operations function that is not in the room when the go-to-market decision is made.

Two-sided businesses, where the plan must be written twice and sequenced once

Marudhar Agri Networks, which connects farmer producer organisations in Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh with institutional buyers, faced the canonical version of this problem: two distinct ideal customer profiles, two channels (field agents for supply, inside sales for demand), two prices (a 2% take rate from buyers, nothing from sellers) and a sequencing question with no symmetric answer. The standard advice — subsidise the harder side — is correct but under-specified, because it does not say how much or for how long. The version an expert uses is a unit calculation: the subsidy is worth paying while the lifetime contribution of the marginal participant on the other side exceeds the subsidy. Marudhar found that each additional producer organisation onboarded raised buyer retention measurably only up to about eleven organisations per crop-district; beyond that, additional supply produced no measurable lift in buyer behaviour. That number turned an open-ended subsidy into a stopping rule, and the stopping rule is the go-to-market strategy. The generalisable failure in two-sided go-to-market is not choosing the wrong side to subsidise; it is never defining the density at which the subsidy stops being purchased growth and starts being purchased revenue.

Regulated markets, where the channel is chosen for you

Maitri Health Cloud sold clinical-documentation software to hospital chains and, later, a patient-facing module. The first product's go-to-market was ordinary enterprise work. The second ran into a constraint no frontier calculation surfaces: consent, data-localisation and clinical-liability rules meant that the patient-facing module could only be distributed through the hospital that held the clinical relationship, which converted a direct-to-consumer product into a channel product with a single intermediary who had no particular incentive to promote it. The lesson generalises beyond health: in insurance distribution, in lending, in pharmaceuticals, in anything touching payments, the set of legal channels is a proper subset of the set of economically attractive ones, and the intersection is sometimes empty. The expert habit is to establish the legal channel set before the economic one, because discovering the constraint afterwards invalidates the whole model rather than adjusting it.

Hardware plus software, where the plan is a financing decision

Matsya's situation is the general case for connected hardware, and Figure 2 is the general shape. Once a device is bundled into a subscription, the go-to-market decision silently becomes a decision about who finances the device: the company, the customer, a partner, or a lender. Mature firms in this position almost always end up separating the two flows — selling or leasing the hardware at or near cost through a financing arrangement and running the subscription as a clean software line — and they usually arrive there after two or three years of trying to make the bundled version work, because the bundled version is easier to sell and the cash consequences lag the sales success by eighteen months. The diagnostic that catches it early is unglamorous: plot cumulative cash per cohort, not per period, and look at whether the curve for the most recent cohort is deeper than the one before it. Growth in a cash-negative unit model looks exactly like success on the revenue line and exactly like distress on the bank statement.

AI-native products, where the marginal cost is real and falling

The Munim case introduces a variable that almost no go-to-market convention was designed for: a cost of service that is material, usage-dependent, and declining rapidly for reasons outside the firm's control. Three consequences follow. Unlimited-use pricing transfers an uncontrolled cost risk to the vendor, so packaging tends towards credits, caps or per-task pricing — and per-task pricing collides with the buyer's desire for a predictable invoice. Free tiers become a genuine budget line, subject to the same scrutiny as paid media, and should be capped by a metric that correlates with cost rather than with time. And because inference prices fall, a price set today against today's margin may be defensible at a lower level next year, which turns pricing into an explicit forecast about someone else's cost curve. Kabir's team had priced at ₹4,000 partly because it produced a tolerable margin at current inference costs; if those costs halve, the same price becomes a 77% gross margin and an invitation to a competitor. An expert would state that assumption in the plan rather than leaving it to be discovered.

The organisational seams, where plans go to be quietly rewritten

The last edge case is not a market type at all. It is the gap between the go-to-market strategy as written and the go-to-market strategy as executed, which is produced not by insubordination but by five ordinary mechanisms that are each owned by someone who was not in the room. Figure 3. Five mechanisms rewrite a go-to-market plan between its approval and its execution. None of them is owned by the person who wrote the plan, and each is individually reasonable. Matsya’s written plan and its effective plan differed by 18% on realised price and by 29 percentage points on analytics attach — a gap large enough to move the company from above the field-sales feasibility curve to below it.

None of the five mechanisms in Figure 3 is a failure of discipline. Each is a reasonable local decision by a competent owner. Together they constitute the company's real go-to-market strategy, and the document that was approved by the board constitutes an intention. The practical implication is that a go-to-market plan should be written with an explicit list of the downstream mechanisms it requires to be changed, and the change should be dated and owned. Plans that end at “segment, channel, price, sequence” are half-written.

6. Ten distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

1. The binding constraint is usually financial, and it moves

A competent practitioner argues about segments and channels. An expert asks, first, what payback period the company can finance, because that single parameter determines which channels exist at all, as Table 2 shows. The tell-tale sign in a live meeting is the sequence of the first two questions: an expert asks about cash before asking about customers, and does so without apology. The obvious reading — that this is finance encroaching on strategy — is wrong, because the constraint genuinely is exogenous to the commercial argument and genuinely does determine it. What makes the distinction subtle is that the constraint moves: a financing round, a working-capital facility secured against contracted revenue, or a shift to annual prepayment can each expand the feasible set overnight. Experts therefore treat the go-to-market plan and the financing plan as one document with two audiences, and revisit the former whenever the latter changes, which is a habit almost nobody has.

2. A channel determines what you can learn about price, not merely what it costs to sell

Every channel is also an instrument for measuring willingness to pay, and the instruments differ enormously in resolution. A self-serve motion yields clean, fast, randomisable price experiments on a population that is unrepresentative of large buyers. A field-sales motion yields negotiated outcomes on exactly the buyers who matter, contaminated by the representative's incentives and impossible to randomise. The tell-tale sign of an expert is that they design the channel partly for what it will teach them: Munim's self-serve tier was worth keeping, on this reading, not because of the revenue it produced but because it was the only place in the business where a price could be tested without a human confounding it. The obvious reading — that price research is a separate activity conducted by surveys — is wrong in practice, because stated willingness to pay in an interview is a weak predictor and the channel is where the real data lives.

3. The first segment should be chosen for the transferability of its reference

The beachhead argument is usually taught as “pick a narrow segment.” The operative property is not narrowness but whether a win inside it makes the next win cheaper. Two segments of identical size can differ by a factor of five in reference transferability: pharmaceutical distributors attend the same three industry associations, use the same four consultants and audit each other's compliance practices, while a set of similarly-sized manufacturers in unrelated categories never speak. The tell-tale question an expert asks is not “how big is this segment” but “when we win this account, who hears about it, and through what mechanism.” The obvious reading — that any focused segment produces word of mouth — is wrong; word of mouth is a property of the social structure of the segment, not of the customer's satisfaction, and satisfaction without a conduit produces no compounding at all.

4. Attach rate is a property of the channel, not of the product

Matsya's analytics module attached at 41% through direct sales and 12% through dealers, which is a difference of the same order as the difference between a good product and a bad one. Practitioners routinely attribute attach failure to packaging or to the module's value, and then rebuild the module. An expert looks first at who is doing the selling and what they are paid for, because a channel that is compensated on device count will sell device count with great skill and will not mention anything else. The tell-tale sign is an attach rate that differs sharply across channels while product satisfaction does not. The obvious reading — that the module needs better positioning — is wrong; the module needs a different incentive on the other side of the conversation, or a packaging change that removes the need for anyone to sell it separately at all.

5. Sequencing is the only free variable, and it is less reversible than it looks

Segment, channel and price are mutually constrained; the order in which a firm addresses segments is genuinely open. But the freedom is exercised once. The second segment inherits the product the first segment shaped, the support model the first segment's expectations created, the brand association the first segment's logos produced, and the sales team's instincts about what a good deal looks like. A company that sells to large pharmaceutical distributors for three years acquires an organisational metabolism — nine-month cycles, custom integrations, a support desk that answers in four hours — that makes a subsequent move to small frozen-food operators far harder than the market analysis suggests. The tell-tale sign of an expert is that they discuss the second segment's requirements while designing the first segment's product and support commitments, treating sequence as a constraint on early design rather than a later decision.

6. The discount matrix is the price list

A published price that is discounted on 80% of deals at an average of 18% is not a price; it is an opening position, and the effective price is set by whoever approves discounts and under what rule. Experts read the approval matrix before they read the pricing page, and they treat changes to discount authority as pricing changes requiring the same scrutiny. The tell-tale sign is a practitioner who, asked what the product costs, answers with a distribution rather than a number. The obvious reading — that discounting is a sales-hygiene problem to be solved with discipline — is wrong most of the time: persistent discounting at a stable level is a market's way of telling a company its list price is above the buyer's reservation price for the configuration being offered, and the correct response is usually to change the packaging so that the discounted configuration becomes a named tier.

7. Blended metrics conceal cohort deterioration, which is the thing you need to see

Blended customer acquisition cost mixes a mature, efficient motion with a new, inefficient one and reports an average that is true of nobody. The number that matters is the trend across acquisition cohorts: is the cost of the customers acquired this quarter higher than last quarter's, and is their retention worse? Munim's blended CAC looked stable across three quarters while the self-serve cohort's CAC rose 31% and the improvement came entirely from a small number of practice-channel deals. The tell-tale sign of an expert is that they ask for the metric split by cohort and by motion before they ask whether it is good. Catching cohort deterioration two quarters late typically costs a company a full hiring cycle spent scaling a motion whose economics had already turned.

8. Win-loss data is a biased sample; the expensive losses never entered the pipeline

Analysing closed-lost deals is valuable and systematically misleading, because it can only tell a company about buyers who considered it. The larger error — a segment that never evaluates you, a channel where you are absent, a positioning that fails to register — leaves no trace in the customer relationship management system. The tell-tale sign of an expert is that they commission non-consideration research: contacting firms that match the ideal customer profile, bought a competing product, and never spoke to the company at all. When Matsya ran twelve such conversations, nine of the twelve had never heard of it, which is a different problem from losing on price and would never have appeared in any loss report. The obvious reading — that low awareness is a marketing problem to be fixed later — is wrong when it is concentrated in one segment, because it means the channel choice for that segment is not underperforming but absent.

9. The competitor that sets your price is usually not a competitor

In most business markets the realistic alternative to buying is not a rival product but a spreadsheet, a junior analyst, an existing internal process or doing nothing at all, and the price ceiling is set by the cost of that alternative rather than by a rival's price card. Munim's real competitor was an article clerk in a chartered-accountancy practice costing ₹18,000 a month, which both sets a ceiling and explains why practices, not businesses, were the natural buyer. The tell-tale sign of an expert is that they can name the specific budget line their price displaces, in the buyer's own accounting vocabulary. The obvious reading — that competitive benchmarking establishes the right price — is wrong whenever the category's penetration is low, because a benchmark against rivals in a market where 90% of prospects buy nothing anchors the price to the preferences of the unusual 10%.

10. Count motions, not channels, and remember that an organisation can run about one

A go-to-market motion is a complete operating system: a way of generating demand, a way of qualifying it, a compensation scheme, a support model, a set of metrics and a hiring profile. Channels are cheap to add on a slide and motions are not, because each one demands a different management attention, a different definition of a good week and often a different kind of person. Below roughly forty commercial employees, a company that attempts two motions simultaneously usually executes neither, and the tell-tale sign is a weekly review in which the same leader is asked to explain both a funnel-conversion number and a pipeline-coverage number and treats one of them as an obligation. The obvious reading — that adding a self-serve channel alongside a sales team is additive because they address different buyers — is wrong at small scale, where the binding resource is not budget but the number of distinct systems the leadership can hold in mind at once.

The differences by stage are sharper than the differences by type, and less often taught. At pre-product-market-fit scale, the go-to-market decision is almost entirely a learning decision: the segment is chosen because it will produce fast, legible feedback, and the price is set partly to find out whether anyone will pay anything. Charging nothing at this stage is defensible only if the company understands it has purchased speed at the cost of the single most informative signal available. At the stage Matsya and Munim occupy — an established motion, a repeatable sale, a question about scaling it — the decision becomes the feasibility and financing problem this page has described, and the danger is confidence: a motion that works at twenty accounts is being extrapolated to two hundred, and the sales learning curve says yield improves while the frontier says the channel may still be under water.

Past roughly a hundred crore of revenue, the problem inverts again. The scarce resource stops being cash or demand and becomes internal coherence: which team sells what, how a new product reaches an installed base without confusing the account team, what happens when two products want different prices from the same customer, and who is allowed to say no to a channel partner. Large companies do not fail at go-to-market because they pick the wrong segment. They fail because eleven reasonable people each optimise their own mechanism and the resulting effective plan — the bottom band of Figure 3 — belongs to nobody. The single most valuable practice in a large firm is therefore a named owner for the coherence of the whole, with the authority to change the compensation plan, and this is rarer than it sounds because it cuts across the usual functional boundaries.

8. Three worked examples, one of them a failure

Maitri Health Cloud: turning a discount habit into a tier

Maitri listed its clinical-documentation product at ₹90 per occupied bed per month. In the year to March 2025, 78% of closed deals carried a discount, at an average of 24%, giving a realised average of ₹68.40 and a list price that the sales team had privately stopped believing in. The instinctive remedies — tighten approval, retrain, hold the line — had each been tried. The diagnostic that worked was to sort discounted deals by what the customer had actually deployed, which revealed that in 71% of discounted deals the hospital used four of the eleven modules and was, quite rationally, refusing to pay for seven it did not want. Maitri introduced a named tier at ₹68 containing exactly those four modules, retained the full product at ₹90, and reduced regional discount authority from 25% to 10%. Over the following three quarters, the share of discounted deals fell to 21%, realised average price per bed rose to ₹74.20 — an 8.5% increase in revenue per bed with no list-price change — and the win rate in competitive evaluations rose by six points, because a cheaper legitimate option beat a grudging discount on the same product. The generalisable mechanism is the one stated in nuance six: persistent discounting is information about packaging, not about discipline.

Milap Learning: a beachhead strategy applied where penetration logic governs

Milap sold a spoken-English practice application to Indian consumers. Its founding team, all of whom had worked in business software, ran a textbook beachhead: a tightly defined first segment of graduates in eight large cities preparing for overseas study, a price of ₹1,499 a quarter, and acquisition through search and social advertising targeted with considerable precision. For five months the numbers were excellent. Cost per install was ₹64, cost per paying subscriber ₹640, and payback under five months. In month six, cost per paying subscriber began to rise, and by month nine it reached ₹1,980 — a payback of sixteen months against a median subscription life of seven. The company had raised ₹22 crore and was spending ₹1.4 crore a month on acquisition.

The failure was not execution. The targeting worked exactly as designed, and that was the problem: the enumerable population of high-intent overseas-study aspirants in those eight cities was roughly 380,000 people, of whom Milap had reached most of the reachable portion within five months. Everything after that was the advertising auction charging a rising price for progressively lower-intent lookalikes. Beachhead logic assumes that winning a narrow segment produces a conduit into an adjacent one; in a consumer category where purchase is individual, low-consideration and socially invisible, no such conduit exists. Milap had imported a framework across the boundary where, as the penetration school insists, it stops holding.

The recovery took fourteen months and cost the company ₹4.6 crore of written-off acquisition spend and two-thirds of its team. What it actually looked like was neither a pivot nor a relaunch but three linked changes: the price moved from ₹1,499 a quarter to ₹399 a month with a one-rupee seven-day trial, which raised trial starts by a factor of nine and cut the decision from a considered purchase to an impulse; the product added Hindi, Marathi and Telugu interface support, extending the addressable population from 380,000 to something in the tens of millions; and, decisively, acquisition shifted away from auction-priced performance advertising towards two owned and earned channels — a preload arrangement with a handset distributor and a programme of regional-language creators paid on a flat monthly retainer rather than per install. Blended acquisition cost per paying subscriber settled at ₹310. Revenue per subscriber fell by 41%; payback fell to 3.2 months; the business worked. The lesson Milap's founders drew, and stated publicly at a conference, was that they had chosen their framework from their own professional history rather than from the structure of the market they had entered.

Manjeera Rail Systems: the plan was fine, the compensation plan was the strategy

Manjeera launched its wagon-utilisation product with a plan for ₹1.1 crore of first-half bookings from its existing twenty-two accounts. It booked ₹28 lakh. Interviews with the eight account executives produced a consistent account: the new product's average deal was ₹9 lakh against ₹46 lakh for the flagship, both carried the same single revenue quota, and introducing a second product mid-cycle risked reopening a procurement conversation on a renewal worth five times as much. Manjeera changed three things: a separate ₹35 lakh quota for the new product, a 2× commission accelerator on it for two quarters, and a rule that the new product could be sold on a two-page amendment rather than a fresh master agreement. Bookings in the following two quarters were ₹94 lakh. Nothing about the segment, the price, the channel or the product changed. The entire difference was in a mechanism that the original go-to-market document had not mentioned, because nobody in the room owned it.
