Three of these deserve amplification because they are chronically misdiagnosed. Beachhead exhaustion presents identically to a marketing performance problem: cost per acquisition rises, everyone blames the agency, the creative is refreshed, and the cost keeps rising. The distinguishing signature is that conversion rates further down the funnel remain stable while cost at the top rises — which means the traffic is no longer worse, it is merely scarcer and therefore dearer. Milap's numbers showed exactly this pattern for four months before anyone interpreted it correctly. The fix is never creative; it is either a new segment or a channel that is not auction-priced.

Channel concentration is misdiagnosed in the opposite direction: it looks like success right up to the moment it does not. The warning sign is not partner revenue growing — that is the intended outcome — but the ratio of partner-sourced revenue to the number of partners sourcing it. Two hundred dealers producing 60% of revenue is a distribution strategy. Fourteen practices producing 60% of revenue is a dependency, and the fourteen will eventually work out that they can ask for a larger share, or build something themselves, or simply switch. Experts negotiate the terms of that eventual conversation early, while they still have the option not to have it.

Effective-plan drift is the most common and the least dramatic. It rarely triggers a crisis; it simply means the company is executing a strategy nobody chose. The cheapest counter-measure is a quarterly reconciliation in which the written plan and the realised numbers are put side by side: intended segment against actual customer mix, intended price against realised price distribution, intended channel against how the last thirty deals actually originated. Companies that do this find divergences of 15% to 30% routinely, and the point of the exercise is not to punish the divergence but to decide, deliberately, which version is now the plan.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Four disagreements in this topic are live among people who are each competent, informed and looking at real evidence. They are not resolved by a synthesis, and a practitioner who pretends otherwise will be caught out by someone who has read the other side.

Beachhead against penetration

The beachhead position holds that early growth is produced by concentration: a segment small enough to dominate produces references, a sharpened product, a repeatable pitch and a conduit into the next segment, and that dominance in a small pond is worth more than presence in a large one. Its evidence is the pattern of successful business-software companies, most of which can point to a first vertical, and the mechanism is plausible and observable — buyers in tight professional communities genuinely do ask each other what they use. The penetration position holds that growth in almost all measured categories comes from increasing the number of light, occasional buyers rather than from deepening relationships with heavy ones, that loyalty metrics are largely a function of market share rather than a cause of it, and that narrow targeting therefore buys less growth per rupee than broad availability. Its evidence is several decades of purchase-panel data across hundreds of categories, which is a far stronger empirical base than the beachhead literature has ever assembled. What would have to be true for the beachhead position to be wrong is that reference effects between customers are weak — and in categories where buyers do not talk to one another, they demonstrably are, which is precisely what happened to Milap. What would have to be true for the penetration position to be wrong is that its evidence base, drawn overwhelmingly from frequently purchased consumer goods, does not transfer to infrequent, high-consideration, committee-mediated purchases — and there is a reasonable case that it does not. The honest position is that the two schools are probably each correct about different regions of the same space, and that the boundary runs somewhere near purchase frequency and social visibility, but nobody has drawn it with any precision.

Whether the AI cost structure is a new regime or a passing artefact

One camp holds that material marginal cost per user is a durable feature of AI-native products, because as inference gets cheaper, products will consume more of it — longer reasoning, more retrieval, more verification passes — and expectations will rise to absorb the saving. On this view, usage-based packaging, hard caps on free tiers and gross margins in the 50s are the new normal, and go-to-market plans should be written for a distributor's economics rather than a software company's. The other camp holds that the current cost structure is a transitional artefact: model prices have fallen by more than an order of magnitude for equivalent capability in successive years, and a company that redesigns its packaging around today's costs will be left with awkward metering in a market where competitors offer simple unlimited plans. Both positions have evidence; they differ in what they extrapolate. The practical test is whether a firm's own cost per successful task is falling faster or slower than the capability its customers demand is rising, and this is measurable in a company's own data within two quarters.

Underpricing as the default error, against land-and-expand

One view, argued most forcefully in the monetisation literature, is that the modal company prices too low, does so because it never asked customers about willingness to pay before building, and then spends its life trapped beneath an anchor of its own making; the remedy is to design the product around a price established in advance. The opposing view is that price is a discovery instrument best used at low settings first, because a low entry price maximises the number of customers from whom you learn, and net revenue retention — expansion within accounts — recovers the margin later. The evidence for the first is a large body of consulting case work and the observable rarity of price increases. The evidence for the second is the performance of companies whose expansion revenue exceeds their new-business revenue. What would have to be true for the land-and-expand view to be wrong is that expansion mechanisms fail to activate — and for products without a natural expansion unit, such as a flat per-company subscription, they systematically do. That is a specific, checkable condition, and it is the most useful thing a practitioner can take from this dispute.

Whether go-to-market should have a single owner

The case for a single owner is coherence: Figure 3 shows what happens without one, and a named leader with authority over pricing, packaging, channel and the sales compensation plan can keep the written and effective plans aligned. The case against is that the decision genuinely requires product, sales, finance, legal and support knowledge that no individual possesses, that a single owner tends to optimise the half they understand, and that the firms which appear to have a strong go-to-market leader usually have a strong cross-functional forum and a leader who chairs it. This one is unresolvable in the abstract because it turns on the specific person available, and experienced executives will say so.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this topic can describe a segment, a channel, a price and a sequence, and will produce a competent document. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in six observable ways.

They begin from the constraint rather than the opportunity. Asked to design a go-to-market plan, they will spend the first hour establishing gross margin, payback tolerance and cash position, and will treat the resulting feasible set as the real content of the exercise. This looks pessimistic to colleagues and is in fact the opposite: it is what allows them to commit hard to the options that remain, instead of hedging across options that were never available.

They write plans that name the mechanisms, not just the intentions. A plan by an expert contains a line about the compensation scheme, a line about discount authority, a line about what support tier each price includes and a date by which each must change. They know that these are where the strategy will actually be decided, and that specifying them is the difference between a decision and a wish.

They quantify to the point where the judgement becomes visible, and then stop. The arithmetic in sections three and eight exists to locate the disagreement, not to resolve it. An expert produces the Matsya cash curve in order to say: here is the point at which this stops being a calculation and becomes a bet about attach rate, and here is who should make that bet. Practitioners who keep producing analysis past that point are usually avoiding the moment of judgement rather than informing it.

They hold the sequence in mind while designing the first step. The support commitment made to the first ten customers, the integration built for the first large account, the tier structure chosen at launch — each is a constraint on the second segment, and an expert prices that constraint at the time rather than discovering it two years later.

They distinguish between what the numbers say and what the numbers can say. They know that win-loss analysis cannot see non-consideration, that blended metrics cannot see cohort deterioration, and that a ratio computed on accounting profit cannot see a cash problem. Much of practical expertise here is a catalogue of what each standard instrument is blind to.

Finally, they revisit. An expert treats the go-to-market plan as having an expiry date, usually two quarters, and schedules the re-decision before it is needed. This is the least glamorous item on the list and probably the highest-yielding, because most of the damage this topic describes is done not by a wrong initial decision but by a right initial decision left in place after the conditions that justified it have changed.

12. What Sudha and Kabir decided

Sudha Ramanathan took a hybrid to her board on 6 May 2026, and was explicit that it was a hybrid because the arithmetic did not support a pure position. Matsya would keep direct field selling for a named list of thirty-one accounts — every pharmaceutical distributor and cold-chain operator whose estimated device requirement exceeded 450 units, where the annual contract value cleared ₹16 lakh and sat comfortably above the field-sales curve even at 45% gross margin. Every account below that threshold would move to the dealer channel, with two changes to the dealer agreement that Joseph Pinto had argued for and won: the dealer margin would rise from 25% to 32% on accounts where the analytics module was attached, making the upsell worth a dealer's effort for the first time, and Matsya would sell the loggers to dealers at ₹4,200 rather than bundling them, removing the working-capital drag entirely for that half of the business. The frozen-foods and dark-store expansion, the line Sudha had struck out in April, was deferred by two quarters and reframed: rather than nine field territories, it would be tested with two dealers in Pune and Coimbatore and a stopping rule of forty accounts before any further commitment. Ritu Bhandare's condition, accepted by the board, was that cumulative cash per cohort would appear in the monthly pack from June onward, on the same page as bookings.

Kabir Sethi's decision was harder because the thing the numbers recommended was the thing he was afraid of. He did not choose. He bounded. Munim would sign a two-year agreement with eight chartered-accountancy practices, capped deliberately at eight so that no practice could exceed 9% of revenue, at ₹1,200 per client workspace with a most-favoured-pricing clause in Munim's favour rather than the practice's. Simultaneously, the free tier would be retained but re-capped — from an invoice-count limit to a limit on reconciliation runs, the metric that actually drives inference cost — which modelling suggested would cut pre-conversion inference cost by 58% while reducing activated free workspaces by only 14%. The direct self-serve motion would continue at reduced spend, justified in the plan on grounds Shalini Koppar found unsatisfying and Kabir considered decisive: it was the only channel in which Munim could run a clean price experiment, and the only place where the company would hear from an end customer who had not been mediated by a practice. Whether eight practices is a channel or the beginning of a dependency is a question Munim will answer in about two years, and Kabir wrote in the board memo that he did not know.

Discussion questions.

  1. Matsya's direct motion is infeasible at a 41% analytics attach rate and feasible at full attach, and Sudha's hybrid resolves the tension by splitting the account base rather than by choosing a side. Under what circumstances is a split motion a legitimate strategy rather than an avoidance of the decision — and what would you need to observe by the end of 2026 to conclude that Matsya had avoided it?
  2. Munim's practice channel wins on customer acquisition cost, payback, retention and revenue, and Kabir caps it at eight partners anyway. Put a number on what that cap costs the company over two years, then state what risk it is buying and whether the price is fair. If you believe the cap is wrong, what would you do instead about the concentration it is designed to prevent?
  3. Milap Learning's founders applied a beachhead framework in a category the penetration school claims it does not fit. Identify one product you know well and state which of the two schools its market structure favours, naming the specific evidence — purchase frequency, social visibility of the purchase, the existence of a reference conduit — that you would gather before committing a budget to either.
